content.title: About
content.content: Liquid coffee creamer is a ready‑to‑use product added to coffee to give it a smoother texture, creamy taste, and aromatic notes. It comes in a variety of flavors such as vanilla, caramel, hazelnut, and more.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Coffee creamer often contains vegetable oils like soy or coconut, plus emulsifiers that keep the mixture homogeneous.
Flavored versions may use natural extracts, but artificial flavorings are common for flavor stability.
Liquid creamer is convenient for office coffee machines because it dissolves instantly without frothing.
In some markets, creamer is sold in single‑serve sachets for one‑time use.

items.title: Mildens coffee bitterness
items.content: Cremers reduce the bitterness and acidity of coffee, making it more palatable for a wide audience.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Certain formulations are fortified with riboflavin (B2) and cobalamin (B12), supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Improves mouthfeel
items.content: Emulsifiers create a velvety, creamy consistency that enhances the drinking experience.

items.title: Soy or dairy allergy
items.content: Many creamers contain soy protein or dairy solids, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Flavored varieties often contain added sugars, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Some creamers use partially hydrogenated oils that contain trans fats, which are harmful to cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add 10–30 ml of creamer to hot coffee, stir, and enjoy. It can also be used in iced coffees, lattes, cappuccinos, and dessert sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator after opening, tightly sealed, and use within 30 days. Do not freeze the product.

egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-made.title: Egg white omelet, scrambled, or fried, made with margarine

content.title: About
content.content: An egg white omelet is a dish made from pure egg whites cooked in margarine. Egg whites are high in protein and virtually fat‑free, while margarine adds flavor and the necessary fat for cooking. The dish can be served as a classic folded omelet, scrambled, or fried pieces, suitable for a lean diet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white is about 90 % water and over 10 % high‑quality protein, mainly albumin.
Margarine was created in the late 19th century as a cheaper alternative to butter.
Egg white omelets are popular in sports nutrition because of their high protein and low calorie profile.
Cooking with margarine gives a crisp edge without adding saturated fats.
Egg whites are easily digested, providing quick satiety and sustained energy.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Egg whites provide about 11 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Pure egg whites contain virtually no fat, making the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: They contain riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3), important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports immune function
items.content: Lysine and other amino acids help in antibody synthesis.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The dish does not cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, beneficial for diabetics.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to egg whites, which can trigger skin or respiratory reactions.

items.title: Trans‑fat content in margarine
items.content: Certain margarines contain trans fats; choose trans‑fat‑free varieties.

items.title: Potential excess sodium
items.content: Margarine is often salted; monitor overall sodium intake.

items.title: Overcooking risk
items.content: Over‑cooking egg proteins can form acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the egg white omelet with sautéed vegetables, herbs, low‑fat cheese, or whole‑grain toast. For scrambled, whisk whites with a splash of water and cook over medium heat, stirring constantly. When frying, use a small amount of margarine to prevent excess greasiness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked omelet in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Raw egg whites keep in their original packaging in the fridge for 3–5 days. Frozen portions can be kept for up to 1 month.

content.title: About
content.content: Grapefruit juice 100% is a completely natural beverage obtained from fresh grapefruits without added sugar, preservatives, or flavorings. It has a bright citrus aroma, a slightly bitter taste, and a high content of vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Grapefruit was developed in the Caribbean in the early 18th century as a hybrid of pomelo and sweet orange.
Grapefruit juice contains more than 30 mg of vitamin C per 100 ml, exceeding the amount in orange juice.
The juice is often used in culinary applications such as marinades, sauces, and cocktails.
It retains most phytochemicals like lycopene and naringenin, which have antioxidant properties.
In some countries grapefruit juice is considered a “superfood” because of its low glycemic index.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: One cup (250 ml) of grapefruit juice provides about 100 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Lycopene and naringenin protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The acidity stimulates gastric juice production, aiding digestion.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Grapefruit juice can increase the effect of certain medications (e.g., statins); consult a doctor when taking prescription drugs.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to citrus fruits.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drink the juice chilled on its own, use it in smoothies, cocktails, marinades, sauces, or add it to tea for a citrus twist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in a sealed container. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days. Discard if the color, smell, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: A zucchini muffin is a moist baked treat that incorporates grated zucchini, flour, eggs, milk, and a modest amount of sugar. The zucchini adds humidity and a subtle vegetable note, making the muffin more nutritious than typical sweet muffins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Zucchini is over 90 % water, which keeps the muffin extra tender.
Unlike many vegetables, zucchini has a very mild flavor, allowing it to pair well with both sweet and spicy ingredients.
Grated zucchini retains most of its vitamins, especially vitamin C and vitamin K.
Zucchini muffins are often used in kids' meals as a way to sneak vegetables into the diet without a strong taste change.
During baking, zucchini releases some moisture, so recipes usually call for a slight increase in dry ingredients.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Zucchini provides vitamin C, vitamin K, potassium, and magnesium, which support immunity, bone health, and heart function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A medium zucchini contains about 20 kcal, so muffins with it are less calorie‑dense than traditional sweet versions.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Carotenoids and lutein in zucchini protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Heart‑friendly nutrients
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help regulate blood pressure and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Wheat or egg allergy
items.content: As with any baked good, muffins can trigger reactions in people allergic to gluten or eggs.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite the vegetable addition, most recipes include sugar; those monitoring blood glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Potential foodborne illness
items.content: If zucchini is left at room temperature too long, bacterial growth can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Zucchini muffins can be enjoyed as a snack, paired with yogurt, cottage cheese, or nut butter. They are convenient for on‑the‑go meals or as part of a child’s lunchbox.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store baked muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days or in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. For longer keeping, freeze them in bags—they retain flavor and texture for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is whole corn kernels that explode when heated, creating a light, airy snack. This ready‑to‑eat version comes pre‑packaged and contains reduced salt (low‑sodium). It has the classic roasted‑corn aroma and a crunchy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the few corn varieties that can “pop” due to the high moisture content inside each kernel.
Native peoples of North and South America traditionally prepared popcorn long before modern microwaves existed.
More than 30 corn varieties are suitable for popping, but only about 5 % of commercially grown hybrids produce a good pop.
Popcorn is a staple in movie theaters; in the United States over 13 billion servings are consumed each year.
Low‑sodium popcorn fits well into sodium‑restricted diets and can be part of a healthy snack routine.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt helps maintain normal blood pressure and lessens the burden on the kidneys.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Popcorn provides dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Compared with many other snacks, popcorn delivers fewer calories per volume.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Corn kernels contain polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Popcorn is naturally free of gluten, making it safe for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Some ready‑to‑eat popcorn varieties may contain artificial flavors or preservatives; always check the label.

items.title: Risk of over‑consumption
items.content: Because it is light and airy, popcorn can be eaten in large quantities, potentially adding extra calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn is ready straight from the package. It can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, mixed with dried fruit or nuts, or used as a crunchy topping for salads and other dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container. For extended shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption that can make it lose its crispness.

yogurt-greek-low-fat-milk-fruit.title: Greek Yogurt, Low Fat Milk, Fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Greek yogurt made from low‑fat milk with added fruit is a thick, creamy dairy product high in protein and low in calories. The fruit provides natural sweetness and a boost of vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt is strained to remove whey, giving it a denser texture than regular yogurt.
Low‑fat milk retains most nutrients while contributing almost no fat.
Fruit is often folded in after fermentation to preserve flavor and vitamins.
Greek yogurt is frequently used as a substitute for sour cream or mayonnaise in recipes.
Regular consumption can support gut health thanks to its probiotic cultures.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Greek yogurt provides up to 10 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using low‑fat milk makes the product virtually fat‑free, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Live bacterial cultures promote a healthy intestinal microbiome.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruit adds vitamin C, potassium and antioxidants, while the milk contributes calcium and vitamin D.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: The combination of probiotics and fruit fiber aids digestion and regular bowel movements.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience discomfort after consuming yogurt.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergy to casein or whey requires complete avoidance of the product.

items.title: Sugar content in fruit
items.content: Certain fruit additions can raise sugar levels, which is important for diabetics to monitor.

items.title: Canned fruit
items.content: If canned fruit is used, it may contain added sugars and preservatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the yogurt as a snack, blend it into smoothies, use it in sauces, desserts, or as a base for dressings. Pair with nuts, honey, or whole grains for a more balanced meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the yogurt in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C in its original container. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.
